case: Tomas is a senior auditor. While closing a client file he finds that his mentor Ruth, who is eleven months from retirement, backdated her signature on a review form by two days so the file would meet a regulatory deadline. The review itself was complete and correct; the backdating changed nothing about the client's finances or the audit opinion. Firm policy and the licensing body both treat a false date on a signed form as misconduct, and a report triggers a mandatory license review that in practice ends careers. Ruth trained Tomas and has never, to his knowledge, done this before.
question: Should Tomas report the backdating?

case: Lena organizes a regional photography prize with five paid judges. One judge, Amir, discloses on the first day that his sister has entered. The rules bar judges from scoring entries by relatives but say nothing about removing them from the panel. Amir offers to abstain on his sister's entry and score the other 240. Scores are averaged across judges, so his abstention slightly changes the weighting of her entry relative to the others, and he will see the other judges' scores on her work before the final round.
question: Should Lena remove Amir from the panel entirely?

case: Hal promised his daughter Ana, in writing, that he would pay her final year of university tuition, and she turned down a paid apprenticeship to finish her degree on that basis. A month before the fees are due, a storm collapses the roof of his son Ben's house; Ben's insurer has denied the claim on a policy exclusion, Ben has a young child, and the repair costs almost exactly the tuition amount. Hal has no other savings and cannot borrow. Ana could defer a year and work; Ben's family would have to move in with Hal for the winter.
question: Should Hal redirect the tuition money to Ben's roof?

case: A published scholarship rule at a public college awards one full grant to the applicant with the highest GPA in the cohort. This year the highest GPA belongs to Mei, whose parents pay her living costs and who has said she would attend without the grant. The second-highest, 0.05 lower, belongs to Dario, who works thirty hours a week and has said he will drop out without it. The committee has discretion under the rule's wording only where GPAs are tied, and they are not.
question: Should the committee award the grant to Mei?

case: Nora's father is in his last days and asks whether his estranged son Kevin, who cut contact five years ago after a bitter argument, has sent any word. Telling him the truth will cause him real grief in the hours he has left; telling him Kevin sent his love would comfort him and can never be found out by him.

case: Elias holds a legal right to draw his full water allocation from the river for his orchard, a right his family has held for sixty years. In the third year of drought, the downstream town's wells are failing and the town has asked upstream users to voluntarily draw half; the state has declined to order it. Drawing his full share keeps his mature trees alive; drawing half loses about a third of them, which takes a decade to replace. The town's shortfall would be covered if the four largest upstream users, of whom Elias is one, all drew half; if only he does, it makes little difference.
question: Should Elias draw his full allocation?

case: Farah runs trust and safety at a marketplace. An automated model has flagged 1,100 seller accounts as part of a scam ring targeting elderly buyers; on past performance about 5% of flags are wrong. Suspending all flagged accounts now stops the scam today; honest sellers caught in the sweep lose sales until a human review clears them, which takes about a week. Reviewing first before suspending anyone takes the same week, during which the ring keeps operating at its current rate of roughly forty victims a day.
